rv.q: I needn’t have worried a nano-second.
This musical adaptation of Robert Zemeckis's hit 1985 time-travel movie is enormous fun.
Whatever its flaws, this musical provides a whacking great hit of spectacle, entertainment and nostalgia – and should leave audiences feeling suitably transported.
Is it a great musical? Absolutely not.
It's possible to ignore the fact that dramaturgically, structurally and emotionally this show is a mess when it offers up such relentless glee and unceasing spectacle.
Once the dazzle of John Rando’s production wears off, though, it all feels a bit pointless.
Despite its inventions and its abundant splashiness, it is an odd mishmash of originality and imitation, the DeLorean remaining its biggest star.
For all the care that’s gone into replicating its source material, what feels most authentic about Back to the Future: The Musical is its capacity for pure spectacle.
It is extra as hell, every scene drenched in song, dance, wild fantasy asides, fourth-wall-breaking irony and other assorted shtick.
John Rando’s West End production is middling at best.

And, in truth, it’s not exactly a musical in the traditional sense. After two viewings, I’d be hard pressed to reproduce much of the original score; the songs that stick are the pop hits used in the movie and triumphantly reprised here, “Johnny B Goode” and “The Power of Love.”
With all its special effects, Back to the Future: The Musical achieves something incredible; it’s not just like watching a Hollywood movie, it’s like being in a Hollywood movie.
Far better to strap yourself in, fire up the flux capacitor and stick the pedal to the metal all the way up to 88mph.
It's undoubtedly an evening that sends you back to your own future with a smile on your face, a perfect night out for nostalgics and car-loving kids of all ages.
The storyline is a thing of exquisite and ingenious beauty.
There’s one jaw-dropping effect in The Future’s finale which has audiences marvelling, “How did they do that?!”
An absolutely electrifying show.
A huge spectacle, this could just be the best show in the West End at the moment.
For me, The Musical will remain an entertaining rather than an exciting experience.
A couple of bland numbers could be ditched to bring it under 2 and ¾ hours but it is still a blast and a half.

cn.t: Critics praise the spectacular stagecraft and eye-popping DeLorean effects, but find the musical additions forgettable. A faithful, fun adaptation that dazzles visually while struggling to justify its existence as a musical.
